clue.text: Burns cakes here

blocks.note: surface reading: a kitchen where something is scorching the baking
setter's reading: Robert Burns, the poet, belongs to the Land of Cakes, an old nickname for his country

explanation.walkthrough: 'Burns' looks like a verb but is the poet Robert Burns. The Land of Cakes is an old nickname for Scotland, from its oatcakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Scotland is the homeland of the poet Robert Burns and was traditionally called the Land of Cakes after its oatcakes.

clue.text: One that remains cool even when framed?

definitions.text: One that remains cool even when framed?

blocks.clueFragment: One that remains cool even when framed?
blocks.note: surface reading: a calm criminal who stays unruffled when set up by the police

blocks.clueFragment: One that remains cool even when framed?
blocks.note: setter's reading: the salad vegetable of the saying 'cool as a ...', which is grown under a glass garden frame

explanation.walkthrough: 'Framed' suggests being falsely accused; here it means grown in a cold frame, a glass-topped box gardeners use for tender plants.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial phrase 'cool as a cucumber' describes calm, and cucumbers are commonly raised in garden cold frames.

clue.text: Hispaniola's game

blocks.note: surface reading: a sport played on the Caribbean island of Hispaniola
setter's reading: the Hispaniola is the schooner in Stevenson's Treasure Island, and her voyage was a quest for buried gold

explanation.walkthrough: Hispaniola reads as the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, but it is the ship in Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: The voyage of the schooner in Stevenson's novel was a search for buried pirate gold, which is also a party game.

clue.text: Old shape, new shape, of everlasting flower

indicators.note: giving something a new shape means remodelling it, so the preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An ageing topiary or vase is being remodelled into the form of an undying bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'shape' is the trick: the first is fodder, the second, with 'new', is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The asphodel is the lily of Greek myth that covers the Elysian meadows, so poets call it an immortal bloom.

clue.text: Speech peculiar? Have to face shock treatment

blocks.note: a dial is the face of a clock, and slang for a person's face
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, an electric shock treatment

explanation.surface: Someone with odd speech is told they must face electric shock therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speech peculiar' is read as 'speech peculiar to a place', not as odd talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A dialect is a form of a language particular to one region or social group, with its own words and pronunciation.

clue.text: Bad temper, even after upsetting records

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting something turns it on its head, so the word for records is read upwards

blocks.note: LPs are long-playing records
e'en is the poetic contraction of even, as in evening

explanation.surface: Someone is in a foul mood, all the more after their vinyl collection is knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' comes after the upset records in the answer, as 'after' says.
explanation.definitionFit: The spleen was once thought the seat of ill humour, so the word still means anger or irritable spite.

clue.text: Tempestuous scene — full of noises

blocks.note: surface reading: a stormy, clamorous place
setter's reading: the setting of Shakespeare's The Tempest, where Caliban says it is full of noises, sounds and sweet airs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tempestuous' means 'of The Tempest', not stormy. Caliban's line is 'Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's play is set on a small island, which Caliban describes as filled with sounds and music.

clue.text: Resolving to write articles on the pound upset the City

definitions.note: adjective sense: resolving things into their elements

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the last word is read from the bottom up

blocks.note: the two indefinite articles, an and a
L is the pound sign, from Latin libra
the word taken as written

explanation.surface: A financial journalist sets out to write pieces about sterling's fall rattling the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, which fits the pound story; here it is just four letters. 'On' places the pound after the articles.
explanation.definitionFit: Analytic means breaking something down into its component parts, which is what resolving a compound or problem does.

clue.text: Confine the young mischief-maker to irons perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word for chains is only one possible arrangement of its letters

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A parent threatens to clap a naughty child in leg irons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irons' is a real way to confine someone, which hides that it is only letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: To imprison someone is to shut them up in a jail or cell, restricting their freedom of movement.

clue.text: Old port measure

blocks.note: first meaning: the ancient harbour city in northern Israel, taken by the Crusaders
second meaning: a unit of land area, 4,840 square yards

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old port' tempts you toward aged wine; it is a historic harbour town on the coast near Haifa.
explanation.definitionFit: Acre is both the Crusader seaport in Galilee and the traditional imperial unit for measuring land area.

clue.text: Mark of Paris shows the weak spot

blocks.note: first meaning, cryptic: the Trojan prince Paris shot the Greek hero with an arrow in the one place he could be wounded
second meaning: a single point of vulnerability

explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark of Paris' sounds like a French brand or the old currency; Paris is the Trojan archer, and the mark is his target.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek hero was invulnerable except at one heel, so the phrase now means anyone's single point of vulnerability.

clue.text: Mark of high degree for Mrs McPherson

blocks.note: at a high temperature, many degrees on the thermometer
St Mark wrote one of the four Gospels

explanation.surface: A high grade is awarded to a particular woman, as on a school report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a grade, and 'high degree' like rank; they are the evangelist and temperature. The pieces come in reverse order of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Aimee Semple McPherson was a flamboyant American revivalist preacher of the 1920s, the very type of fervent evangelist.

clue.text: Article certain to be plentiful

blocks.note: the indefinite article
as in 'bound to happen'

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece is sure to appear in large numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: To abound is to exist in great quantities, so the verb matches being present in large supply.

clue.text: Planck's quantity, like Caesar's quality

blocks.note: first meaning: the fixed physical value h named after the physicist Max Planck
second meaning: steadfast, as Shakespeare's Caesar says 'I am ... as the northern star'

explanation.walkthrough: Two learned allusions, one from quantum physics, one from Julius Caesar, the speech just before his assassination.
explanation.definitionFit: Planck's value is a fixed physical number, and Shakespeare's Caesar boasts of being as unwavering as the Pole Star.

clue.text: Not the army's mess room, this one

definitions.text: Not the army's mess room, this one

blocks.clueFragment: Not the army's mess room, this one
blocks.note: surface reading: some other barracks room, not the one where soldiers eat

blocks.clueFragment: Not the army's mess room, this one
blocks.note: setter's reading: the opposite of a mess is tidy, and the army's company office has that adjective in its name

explanation.walkthrough: A 'mess' is the soldiers' dining hall, but also untidiness; the orderly room is a British army company's office.
explanation.definitionFit: Orderly means neat and tidy, the opposite of a mess, and also names the army office where routine duties are run.

clue.text: Taken off by a painter before he put it on ?

definitions.text: Taken off by a painter before he put it on ?

blocks.clueFragment: Taken off by a painter before he put it on ?
blocks.note: surface reading: some garment or smock a decorator removes and then wears

blocks.clueFragment: Taken off by a painter before he put it on ?
blocks.note: setter's reading: he removes his outdoor coat before working, then applies a top layer of paint

explanation.walkthrough: The paradox resolves because 'it' changes meaning: an outdoor garment taken off, then a final layer of paint put on.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a heavy outer garment worn outdoors and the topmost layer of paint a decorator applies.

clue.text: 14, deplorable description of an invalid

blocks.note: first meaning: unceasing, the answer to 14 across
second meaning: colloquial British for very bad, as in 'the service was ...'

explanation.surface: Someone describes a sick person as permanently and pitiably unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing phrase backs up the first sense: a long-term patient is called a ... invalid.
explanation.definitionFit: Chronic describes an illness that persists for a long time, and informally in Britain it also means dreadful.

clue.text: Captain of the gate excelled at bridge

definitions.text: Captain of the gate excelled at bridge

blocks.clueFragment: Captain of the gate excelled at bridge
blocks.note: surface reading: a gatekeeper who is a champion card player

blocks.clueFragment: Captain of the gate excelled at bridge
blocks.note: setter's reading: Macaulay's Roman hero, 'the Captain of the Gate', who held the bridge over the Tiber against the Etruscans

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' looks like the card game; it is the Sublician bridge in Macaulay's Lays of Ancient Rome, once learned by heart in British schools.
explanation.definitionFit: In Macaulay's poem the Roman soldier, called the Captain of the Gate, defended the bridge single-handed against an army.

clue.text: I train madly in right surroundings, bringing me to scratch

definitions.note: phrase describing the noun: something that makes me itch

indicators.note: doing something madly means wildly and without order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: An athlete trains frantically in the right setting to bring themselves up to standard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to scratch' means fit enough; here the scratch is literal. The setter places I TRAIN within RT and shuffles the lot, so only the letters matter.
explanation.definitionFit: An irritant is a substance or thing that inflames the skin and causes itching, so it makes a person scratch.

clue.text: Unlike Ophelia's "sweet bells jangled"

blocks.note: surface reading: something unlike the noisy bells of Hamlet
setter's reading: Ophelia says Hamlet's mind is 'like sweet bells jangled, out of tune and harsh', so the opposite is harmonious

explanation.walkthrough: The solver must know how Ophelia's line in Hamlet ends: 'out of tune and harsh'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being brought into harmony, with every bell sounding true, is the reverse of bells that are out of tune.

clue.text: Copper advanced two points at first — can be assimilated 161. 25

definitions.note: phrase for the adjective: able to be digested

blocks.note: E and S, east and south, two compass points
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
advanced as a loan, as in 'advanced me the money'
not clue words: debris from the newspaper scan, ignored

explanation.surface: A police officer is promoted after scoring points on his first attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman and 'advanced' like promotion. 'At first' puts the two points at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Esculent is a formal word for edible, describing food that the body can digest and take in.

clue.text: A hard 15 dn is among the nameless . .

indicators.note: the letters sit among those of the following words, concealed inside them

blocks.note: lies across the two words, losing th- at the start and -ss at the end

explanation.surface: A tough coat lurks unidentified among anonymous people.
explanation.walkthrough: 15 dn is OVERCOAT, so the definition means a hard top coating, as on teeth or pottery. The dots lead into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a glassy protective coating fired onto metal or pottery, and the hard outer layer of a tooth.

clue.text: Official publication about drink

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: A government white paper on alcohol is being issued.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is a formal document setting out findings, such as a committee's account published by a government department.

clue.text: Can plan Trout with variations of this kind

indicators.note: a musical theme with variations is restated in altered forms, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A composer plans to write variations on Schubert's Trout.
explanation.walkthrough: Schubert's Trout Quintet has a set of variations, so the surface is musical; 'of this kind' refers back to the variations the clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Contrapuntal music weaves independent melodic lines together, the style of counterpoint used in many sets of variations.

clue.text: . . . ones wrecking this organ

indicators.note: something wrecked is broken up, so the letters of the preceding word are scattered and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Following on from 21, people with no names are ruining their own features.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots continue from 21 down's hidden enamel; this clue stands alone in its parsing.
explanation.definitionFit: The nose is the facial organ of smell and breathing, which is what 'this organ' points to.

clue.text: Look over all doubtful starters — weight to be carried

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initials of the four words

explanation.surface: Someone checks all the doubtful runners before a horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, starters are the runners and the weight carried is the handicap, so the surface reads as a day at the races.
explanation.definitionFit: A load is the burden a person, animal or vehicle has to bear, so it is weight that must be carried.

clue.text: Bunthorne confessed that he was a sham one

definitions.text: Bunthorne confessed that he was a sham one

blocks.clueFragment: Bunthorne confessed that he was a sham one
blocks.note: surface reading: a character owns up to being a fraud

blocks.clueFragment: Bunthorne confessed that he was a sham one
blocks.note: setter's reading: in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience, the poet Bunthorne admits he is only posing as a lover of beauty

explanation.walkthrough: Bunthorne, a satire on Oscar Wilde, sings 'Am I alone and unobserved?' and confesses his devotion to art is affected.
explanation.definitionFit: An aesthete is someone devoted to beauty and art, the pose Bunthorne admits to faking in the operetta.

clue.text: By Land's End is an island that's separate

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of the word land
taken as written
the large Greek island

explanation.surface: Near the far tip of Cornwall there is an island set apart.
explanation.walkthrough: Land's End is the westernmost point of Cornwall, so the phrase pretends to be a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrete means distinct and individually separate, as in discrete units, not to be confused with discreet.
